observed_title: Distance Stability for the Integral Hardy and Carleman Inequalities

topic_relevance.basis: The paper proves explicit deficit identities and distance stability for sharp Hardy/Carleman inequalities, including a theorem that controls a local weighted distance to a virtual extremizer family when no genuine extremizer exists. This directly matches near-extremizer stability/ridigity methods, while the exact estimates concern these integral inequalities rather than the target problem's own inequality.

definitions: For Hf(x)=x⁻¹∫₀ˣ f(t)dt, the Hardy deficit is Δ_H(f)=(p′)^p∫f^p−∫(Hf)^p, where p′=p/(p−1).
The Hardy equality equation p′f=Hf has formal solutions c x^(−1/p), not in Lp(0,∞) unless trivial; these are virtual extremizers.
The Carleman geometric mean is G_f(x)=exp(x⁻¹∫₀ˣlog f(t)dt), with deficit Δ_C(f)=e∫f−∫G_f.
The local distance D_x(f)^2=inf_{c≥0} x⁻¹∫₀ˣ(√(t f(t))−√c)^2dt is the variance of √(t f(t)) on (0,x), equivalently a weighted Hellinger distance to c/t.

assumptions: The proof first assumes f is compactly supported and locally bounded to justify endpoint integrations; the statement then extends to general nonnegative Lp functions by truncation, with infinite terms interpreted in the extended sense.
theorem_cards.statement: With h=Hf and Φ_p(r)=r^p−1−p(r−1)≥0, the deficit has the identity Δ_H(f)=∫₀∞ h(x)^p Φ_p(p′f(x)/h(x)) dx (the integrand is set to zero where h=0). In particular the sharp Hardy inequality follows. For p=2 this specializes to the exact square identity 4∫f²−∫(Hf)²=∫(2f−Hf)².
proof_steps: Put F(x)=∫₀ˣ f and h=F/x, so h′=(f−h)/x.
Differentiate x h^p and integrate using the compact-support/local-boundedness endpoint conditions to obtain ∫h^p=p′∫ f h^(p−1).
Let r=p′f/h. The previous relation gives ∫(r−1)h^p=0; subtracting this zero term from the deficit produces ∫[r^p−1−p(r−1)]h^p.
Convexity of r↦r^p gives Φ_p≥0; p=2 gives Φ_2=(r−1)^2 and hence the residual square.
gaps: The endpoint integration proof is first justified for compactly supported, locally bounded f; passage to arbitrary nonnegative Lp data is stated as standard truncation and not detailed in the paper.
This is an exact deficit identity for this Hardy averaging operator, not a general metric stability theorem for arbitrary sharp inequalities.
The formal equality family is not contained in Lp(0,∞), so global Lp distance to a nonzero extremizer is not appropriate.
theorem_cards.author_claim: Theorem 1 identifies the deficit with a nonnegative convexity remainder; Theorem 2 gives the p=2 square identity.
theorem_cards.checked_derivation: I checked the derivative, endpoint integration, cancellation of ∫(r−1)h^p, and p=2 specialization. PDF page 4 was visually checked for equations (4)–(5) and the exact square; the derivation is separate from the author’s unexpanded truncation argument.

assumptions: log f is integrable on every finite interval.
theorem_cards.statement: Define D_x(f)^2=inf_{c≥0} x⁻¹∫₀ˣ(√(t f(t))−√c)^2dt. Then the Carleman deficit obeys Δ_C(f)≥e∫₀∞ D_x(f)^2 dx/x. The distance vanishes on an interval exactly when tf(t) is almost everywhere constant there, i.e. f(t)=c/t there.
proof_steps: First use the stability form of AM–GM: for u>0, its arithmetic mean A and geometric mean M satisfy A−M≥x⁻¹∫₀ˣ(√u−√M)^2.
Set u(t)=t f(t); since x⁻¹∫₀ˣlog t=log x−1, its geometric mean is M(x)=xG_f(x)/e.
Tonelli and the exact tail integral ∫_t^∞ x^(−2)dx=1/t show ∫₀∞ A(x)dx/x=∫₀∞f(t)dt; therefore Δ_C=e∫(A−M)dx/x.
Apply the AM–GM stability lemma at each x; the comparison value √M(x) is one admissible constant in D_x, so the squared error dominates D_x(f)^2 and integration gives the result.
Minimizing over constants identifies D_x² as the variance of √(tf) and yields the equality condition stated in the remark.
gaps: The result uses strict positivity of f and local integrability of log f as well as global L1 integrability; it does not state a version for arbitrary nonnegative f with zeros.
The proof exchanges nonnegative integrals using Tonelli and uses a specific exact tail identity; the corresponding discrete inequality does not retain the same exact remainder, as the author notes.
The distance is local in x and integrated with dx/x; it does not imply a single global Lp closeness to a non-integrable extremizer c/t.
theorem_cards.author_claim: Theorem 3 proves a global deficit lower bound by the scale-integrated local weighted Hellinger distance to c/t; Remark 3 rewrites that distance as a variance.
theorem_cards.checked_derivation: PDF pages 6 and 7 were visually inspected. I checked the weighted substitution u=tf, the factor M=xG_f/e, Tonelli’s kernel ∫_t∞x⁻²dx=1/t, the comparison with the infimum D_x, and the variance minimizer α_x=average √(tf).

constant_dependence: The Hardy identity is exact for each p>1, with the convex remainder Φ_p; for p=2 the coefficient is exactly one on ∫(2f−Hf)². The Carleman distance inequality has coefficient e and no dimension parameter. The optional local Poincaré estimate in Remark 2 depends quadratically on the chosen logarithmic interval length |I|²/π²; it is not a global coercivity constant.
endpoint_limits: Both inequality sharp constants are not attained by nonzero functions in their natural spaces; the equality profiles are virtual extremizers.
For p=2, the deficit controls a residual and, after logarithmic change of variables, only a local distance on finite logarithmic intervals; the profile itself is not globally L².
For Carleman, c/t is not globally integrable; the valid stability metric is the scale-local weighted distance D_x integrated with dx/x.
The Carleman proof relies on the exact continuous tail identity; the paper says the discrete analogue generally yields only an estimate and less tidy weights.
reusable_methods: For an inequality without an attained optimizer, solve its equality equation and identify a virtual-extremizer family before defining a stability metric.
Search for a deficit identity by differentiating a weighted primitive, integrating by parts with explicit endpoint assumptions, and subtracting a zero residual moment to expose a convexity gap.
For an averaged inequality, compare the deficit integrand to a local distance at each scale, then integrate through Tonelli; verify the exact tail kernel before asserting the global coefficient.
Use logarithmic coordinates when scaling creates a translation-invariant defect, and restrict Poincaré control to finite intervals when the extremizer is not globally integrable.
unchecked: The general truncation extension in Theorem 1 is stated but not elaborated; I did not supply a separate proof of the limiting passage.
The Bianchi–Egnell references and related literature were not independently reviewed; the paper’s own proofs and claims were read in full.
PDF pages 4, 6, and 7 were visually checked for principal formulas/proofs; other pages were read as page-structured text without image-by-image comparison.
